title: API 510 Training in Midland, TX: Vessel Inspector Exam Prep
description: Self-paced API 510 exam prep for Permian Basin vessel inspectors: gas plant separators, amine towers, cryogenic vessels and exchangers. Instructor Q&A.
h1: API 510 Training in Midland: Pressure Vessel Inspector Exam Prep for Permian Basin Gas Plants and Refineries
html:
API 510 exam prep for pressure vessel inspectors in the Permian Basin

Most of the pressure vessels around Midland do not sit inside a refinery. They stand in gas processing plants spread across the Midland Basin, at compressor stations and NGL facilities, and in the shops that build and repair them. This page is for the people doing that work, or aiming to, who are preparing for the API 510 pressure vessel inspector examination.

There is no Atlantis classroom in Midland. Atlantis offers API 510 exam preparation as a self-paced online course with an instructor who answers questions, which suits people who spend their days driving between sites rather than sitting near a training room. The American Petroleum Institute decides who is eligible, administers the examination at Prometric test centres and issues the API 510 certification. The course prepares you for that examination; it is not approved by API and does not certify anyone.

Gas plants around Midland, and the vessels inside them

The Midland Basin's processing capacity has grown plant by plant as production rose. Enterprise Products started its Leonidas plant in Midland County in 2024, designed to process more than 300 million cubic feet of gas a day and extract more than 40,000 barrels a day of NGLs, and said its Orion plant would follow in the same basin. In 2025 the company announced Athena as its ninth Midland Basin plant and said that, with Athena running, its Midland Basin assets would have about 2.2 billion cubic feet a day of processing capacity. Targa Resources brought its Greenwood II plant in the Midland Basin online in October 2024 and its East Driver plant in the second quarter of 2026, each rated at 275 million cubic feet a day. Energy Transfer took on eight operating plants and more than 6,000 miles of gathering pipe when it bought WTG Midstream in 2024, with assets in Martin, Howard, Upton, Reagan and Irion counties.

Inside the fence, a cryogenic gas plant is a sequence of pressure vessels. An API 510 candidate from Midland should be able to name the damage each stage of a typical train invites:

  • Inlet separation. Slug catchers and inlet separators receive wet field gas with free water, condensate, carbon dioxide and, on many systems, hydrogen sulfide.
  • Amine treating. The contactor, flash drum, lean and rich amine exchangers, regenerator and reflux accumulator strip out acid gas, and they are where amine stress corrosion cracking and wet hydrogen sulfide damage are studied for the exam.
  • Dehydration. Molecular sieve vessels swing between adsorption and hot regeneration, so the nozzles, supports and welds that take the thermal cycling deserve attention.
  • Cryogenic recovery. Expander separators and the demethanizer run far below ambient temperature, which brings minimum design metal temperature and impact testing into the inspector's working day.
  • Product and refrigeration. NGL surge drums, propane refrigeration accumulators and the shell-and-tube exchangers between them hold light hydrocarbons that can auto-refrigerate if they leak.

Refineries within reach of Midland

Refinery vessel work, with its hydroprocessing reactors, FCC vessels and crude columns, is not on Midland's doorstep. EIA's 2026 refinery capacity report lists three plants within driving distance of the basin:

Three refineries for a whole basin is a short list, so many Midland API 510 holders spend their careers in gas plants, NGL facilities and contract inspection firms rather than in refining. That matters for the exam, because API 510 and its Body of Knowledge were written around refining and chemical process vessels. A gas plant inspector usually has to put real time into topics such as high-temperature hydrogen attack, sulfidation and naphthenic acid corrosion, which are tested but rarely seen on the job.

Production vessels, and where API 510 changes its rules

Out on the leases, separators, heater treaters, free-water knockouts and compressor station scrubbers are pressure vessels too, but API 510 has long handled them differently. Its 2006 edition allowed vessels in exploration and production service, covering drilling, producing, gathering, lease processing and the treating of oil, gas and associated brine, to be inspected under the alternative rules of Section 9, which were written with oil and gas regulators in mind. The API 510 Body of Knowledge in force as this page was written calls that section the rules for natural resource vessels, and it excludes Section 9 and Appendix E from the examination.

Two practical points follow for a Midland candidate. First, the exam tests the general rules, including internal and on-stream interval limits, remaining-life arithmetic, repairs, alterations and rerating, so years of field work on production vessels do not cover the syllabus on their own. Second, whether a particular lease vessel is inspected to API 510 at all is the owner's decision, not the inspector's.

Texas adds a requirement that reaches vessels in sour service. The Railroad Commission's Statewide Rule 36 applies to oil, gas and brine operations, including production, gathering, processing and storage, where the gas contains hydrogen sulfide and the rule's thresholds are met; refineries and petrochemical plants are outside it. For new construction and modifications, it requires metal components chosen to resist sulfide stress cracking, citing NACE MR-01-75 and API RP 14E. An inspector reviewing repairs on a sour plant needs to know it exists, although Rule 36 is not on the API 510 paper.

Damage mechanisms a Permian vessel inspector studies first

The API 510 Body of Knowledge does not test the whole of API RP 571. It lists a set of damage mechanism sections, and several of them are everyday Permian problems:

  • Amine stress corrosion cracking (RP 571 section 3.3). Cracking at carbon steel welds and heat-affected zones in amine service, controlled mainly by post-weld heat treatment. Regenerators, reboilers and lean amine equipment are the places to think of first.
  • Wet H2S damage (section 3.67). Blistering, hydrogen-induced cracking, stress-oriented HIC and sulfide stress cracking in water-wet sour service, typical of inlet separators and the rich side of an amine unit.
  • Brittle fracture (section 3.11). Relevant to cryogenic sections, to vessels that can chill during a blowdown or a leak of light hydrocarbons, and to hydrotests on cold winter mornings.
  • Corrosion under insulation (section 3.22) and chloride stress corrosion cracking (section 3.17). Insulated cold vessels sweat, and insulated stainless steel can crack where chlorides concentrate.
  • Erosion and erosion-corrosion (section 3.27). Inlet nozzles and impingement plates on separators that take sand-laden or high-velocity flow.

Two mechanisms that dominate field corrosion in the basin are missing from the API 510 list: carbon dioxide corrosion and microbiologically influenced corrosion. Both matter on the job, but for the 510 exam the study hours belong to the sections that are tested. MIC does appear in the API 570 and API 653 bodies of knowledge, one reason Midland inspectors often find the piping and tank papers closer to their daily work.

Worked example: the lower shell of an amine regenerator

Here is the kind of calculation the API 510 exam expects, set on a vessel a Midland inspector could meet. The shell is SA-516 Grade 70, 60 in. inside diameter, designed for 250 psi at a temperature where the allowable stress is 20,000 psi, with spot-examined longitudinal seams, so the joint efficiency is 0.85.

  1. Required thickness. ASME Section VIII, Division 1 gives t = PR / (SE − 0.6P) for circumferential stress in a cylindrical shell. With R = 30 in., t = (250 × 30) / (20,000 × 0.85 − 0.6 × 250) = 7,500 / 16,850 = 0.445 in.
  2. Corrosion rates. The thinnest CML read 0.630 in. at the 2014 baseline, 0.580 in. in 2020 and 0.520 in. in 2026. Long-term rate: (0.630 − 0.520) / 12 = 0.0092 in. a year. Short-term rate: (0.580 − 0.520) / 6 = 0.0100 in. a year. API 510 asks the inspector, with a corrosion specialist, to use the rate that best reflects current conditions, which here is the faster short-term figure.
  3. Remaining life. (0.520 − 0.445) / 0.0100 = 7.5 years.
  4. Interval. Unless an RBI assessment justifies something else, the internal or on-stream interval is the lesser of half the remaining life and 10 years, so 3.75 years. Had the remaining life been under four years, API 510 would allow the full remaining life, up to a maximum of two years.

A short-term rate faster than the long-term one also says something changed: heavier acid gas loading, a build-up of heat-stable salts, a hotter reboiler or a more sour gas coming in from new wells. On the exam you simply pick the governing rate. On the job you also ask the process engineer why it moved.

Who sits API 510 from Midland, and the route each takes

API's education and experience rules are the same in Midland as anywhere: one year of inspection with an engineering or technology degree, two years with a two-year degree or technical certificate, three with a high school diploma and five or more with no formal education, all gained in the last ten years while employed by or under contract to an authorized inspection agency. The API 510 certification page sets them out in full. What differs locally is the work people bring with them:

  • Midstream engineers. Mechanical and facilities engineers at gas processing companies often qualify on the one-year route once they have performed or supervised inspection. UT Permian Basin offers bachelor's degrees in mechanical engineering, accredited by ABET, and in petroleum engineering.
  • NDT technicians. UT thickness technicians who have worked plant CML programmes already have inspection hours, and many add API 510 to move from taking readings to evaluating them.
  • Welders and shop QC staff. If you work in a shop that builds or repairs vessels to Section VIII, that construction and repair work counts towards the longer routes, alongside at least a year of inspection.
  • Plant operators. Operators moving into mechanical integrity bring operating experience but usually need a year of hands-on inspection before they apply.

Whether hours on production vessels count is API's decision, made from your application. Describe the equipment, your role and your employer accurately and let API judge it.

Studying API 510 from a Midland schedule

A contractor's inspector in the Permian can cover several plants in a week with long drives between them, and plant staff work shifts that do not line up with evening classes. A self-paced course fits that pattern: you study when you are off site and send questions to the instructor as they arise. A workable order for a gas plant inspector:

  1. Start with API 510 itself, because the interval, repair and rerating rules are the part least like daily field work.
  2. Work the Section VIII calculations next, from shells and heads to MAWP, static head and test pressure, using the code PDF the way the open-book half requires.
  3. Take the tested RP 571 sections one at a time, linking each to a vessel you know, then move on to RP 572, RP 576, RP 577 and RP 578.
  4. Finish with Section V, Section IX and PCC-2, which reward fast look-ups, and then sit timed practice papers under exam conditions.

API runs the examination in set windows, each with its own application deadline and its own effectivity sheet of code editions. Check the current ones on the API exam schedule page before you plan backwards from a target date.

Preparation options in the Permian, compared

Midland has plenty of technical training, but most of it is aimed at operating and building the plants rather than at the API inspector examinations:

  • Midland College runs an Associate of Applied Science in Petroleum Energy Technology with two technician certificates, plus a natural gas compression programme. These build operating knowledge; whether yours counts as a two-year degree or certificate in engineering or technology is for API to decide.
  • Odessa College offers an AAS in welding and continuing-education preparation for the AWS CWI, CWE and CWS examinations, a common first inspection credential for welders.
  • Employer programmes. Larger producers and midstream companies train their own integrity staff and sometimes sponsor API candidates.
  • Classroom exam-prep courses. Private training firms run them, mostly in the larger refining centres, and they suit people who can leave the basin for a stretch.

Atlantis's API 510 course is the self-paced alternative to that classroom model, with instructor Q&A and no fixed dates. If you also need NDT certification, the NDT training in Midland page describes ASNT SNT-TC-1A training for Midland candidates, and the AWS CWI exam-prep course has its own page.

Sponsoring API 510 candidates from a Permian gas plant or contractor

For an operator, an API 510 inspector on staff means vessel evaluations, repair reviews and interval decisions can be made without waiting for a contractor to drive out. For an inspection contractor, it means a crew lead who can sign the evaluation as well as take the readings. Employers can enrol several candidates on one quote. Pairing each candidate with a plant whose vessel files they can study gives the course's worked examples a real counterpart. Fees are quoted on request: tell Atlantis how many candidates you have and when they hope to sit.

faq.q: Is there an API 510 course I can attend in Midland?
faq.a: There is no Atlantis classroom in Midland. The API 510 course is self-paced online with instructor Q&A, so you can study from home, a plant office or a motel between sites. API administers the examination itself, in person at Prometric test centres, and issues the certification to candidates who pass. Prometric's site locator shows the centres closest to Midland; check it once API has accepted your application.

faq.q: Does experience on lease separators and heater treaters count toward API 510?
faq.a: It may, but API decides, not the course provider or your employer. API reviews the education and experience on your application, and the experience has to have been gained while employed by or under contract to an authorized inspection agency. Describe the vessels, the service and what you actually did, whether that was inspection, repair or operation.

faq.q: Is API 510 Section 9 on the exam?
faq.a: Not in the Body of Knowledge in force as this page was written: it excludes Section 9, which it calls the rules for natural resource vessels, along with Appendix E. Each window has its own Body of Knowledge, so check yours. The general interval, repair and rerating rules are fully examined and deserve the time instead.

faq.q: Which damage mechanisms should a gas plant inspector focus on for API 510?
faq.a: Start with the tested RP 571 sections you meet at work: amine stress corrosion cracking, wet H2S damage, brittle fracture, corrosion under insulation, chloride stress corrosion cracking and erosion. Then cover the refinery mechanisms on the list that you may never have seen, such as sulfidation, high-temperature hydrogen attack and naphthenic acid corrosion, because the exam does not weight questions by what is common in the Permian.

faq.q: Do I need an engineering degree to sit API 510?
faq.a: No. A bachelor's degree in engineering or technology shortens the experience requirement to one year of inspection, but API also accepts two-year degrees and technical certificates, a high school diploma or no formal education, with progressively more experience. Military technical service can substitute in some routes. The certification requirements page sets out each combination.

faq.q: Should a gas plant inspector take API 510 or API 570 first?
faq.a: Follow your work. If you spend most of your time on separators, towers and exchangers, API 510 fits; if your programme is mostly circuits, CMLs and injection points, API 570 is the closer match, and its Body of Knowledge includes MIC and soil corrosion. Many Permian inspectors eventually hold both. The API 570 course page describes that paper.

faq.q: Can a midstream company enrol a group of vessel inspectors?
faq.a: Yes. Employers can enrol several candidates together on one quote, and each candidate studies at their own pace with access to the instructor. Each candidate still applies to API individually, and API checks each person's eligibility separately. Fees are quoted on request.
